clue.text: Red and blue housing or a research facility

indicators.note: to house something is to give it shelter inside, so the pieces either side enclose another

parts.note: LAB is short for Labour, the British party whose colour is red
taken as written
taken as written
blue is the colour of the Conservatives, whose members are Tories

explanation.surface: A building painted in red and blue, perhaps housing a science lab.
explanation.walkthrough: In British politics Labour is red and the Conservatives (Tories) blue; the two parties sit either side of OR A, giving LAB-ORA-TORY.
explanation.definitionFit: A laboratory is a room or building equipped for scientific experiments, which makes it a plain synonym for a research facility.

clue.text: Vegetable in bottom of boat brought up

indicators.note: in a down entry, bringing a word up lifts its end to the top, so it reads backwards

parts.note: the keel is the structural spine along the bottom of a boat

explanation.surface: Something green found lying in the bilge of a boat after it was hauled up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brought up' suggests lifting the vegetable from the boat, but it reverses KEEL in this down clue to give LEEK.
explanation.definitionFit: The leek is an onion-family plant grown and eaten as a vegetable, so this is a simple example of the category.

clue.text: Work of art in pieces

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a sculpture of the head and shoulders
second meaning: broken, as in informal speech

explanation.surface: A sculpture or painting found smashed to bits.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one damaged artwork; the clue is two separate meanings of one short word.
explanation.definitionFit: A sculpted head and shoulders is a classic artwork, and colloquially anything broken beyond use is described with the same word.

clue.text: Surprising lack of communication from Icelander, so I gathered

indicators.note: something surprising is unexpected, so the letters turn up in an unexpected order
things gathered are collected together into a heap, so the letters are bundled up and remixed

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that an Icelander has gone surprisingly quiet, or so they gathered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'So I gathered' reads as a casual aside, but it supplies letters and a second anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Radio silence is the deliberate halt of transmissions, and by extension any period without contact or news from someone.

clue.text: Fly goes down into middle of gateau

indicators.note: going into something means ending up inside it
the middle of a word means only its central letters are kept

parts.note: the two central letters of the six-letter cake
the sun sets when it goes down below the horizon

explanation.surface: A fly lands on the middle of a cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes down' is not about the fly descending; it is SETS, as the sun does, placed inside the centre of GATEAU.
explanation.definitionFit: The tsetse is an African biting insect that spreads sleeping sickness, so it is a particular species of fly.

clue.text: Animal coloured in red, always

indicators.note: colouring in a shape means filling its outline, so one word fills the gap inside another

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
e'er is the poetic contraction of ever

explanation.surface: A creature that is always painted red, like Rudolph's nose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coloured in red' sounds like a paint job, but 'coloured' means filled in, as a child colours in an outline; e'er is the poetic form of ever.
explanation.definitionFit: The reindeer is an Arctic deer, so it is simply one example of an animal, and red-nosed Rudolph is a famous one.

clue.text: Comfortable when weapons returned

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: guns are firearms, a common kind of weapon

explanation.surface: Feeling at ease once the arms have been handed back after a conflict.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returned' sounds like a weapons amnesty but it simply flips the word for weapons.
explanation.definitionFit: Snug describes being warm, cosy and at ease, making it a close synonym of comfortable.

clue.text: Getting to squeeze part — very tight?

indicators.note: squeezing something is gripping it tightly, so one piece holds another inside

parts.note: nailing is catching or getting hold of someone
a bit is a part or piece

explanation.surface: Trying to squeeze into a part of a garment that is too tight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very tight' looks like a description of clothing; it means a contest so evenly matched that it is tense.
explanation.definitionFit: A close finish makes spectators anxious enough to chew their fingertips, so nail-biting describes a contest decided by a tight margin.

clue.text: Sour thing sandwiched by cupcake and sweetie?

definitions.text: Sour thing sandwiched by cupcake and sweetie?

parts.words: Sour thing sandwiched by cupcake and sweetie?
parts.note: surface reading: a tart filling between two sweet treats in a dessert
setter's reading: two lovers calling each other pet names, with an unwanted third person stuck between them

explanation.surface: A tart fruit layered between a cupcake and a sweet, like an odd dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: Cupcake and sweetie are terms of endearment, so they stand for a couple; to play the sour fruit is British slang for being the awkward third wheel.
explanation.definitionFit: The tart green fruit gives its name to the British idiom for an unwanted companion who spoils a couple's privacy.

clue.text: Seaside toy tampered with — be careful!

indicators.note: something tampered with has been interfered with and altered, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A warning shouted after someone has interfered with a child's beach toy.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes the warning sound like a response to the tampering, but the toy's letters themselves are what is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a spoken caution urging someone to slow down and proceed gently, the same idea as telling them to take care.

clue.text: Wine quaffed by Romanov in Omsk

indicators.note: what is quaffed is swallowed, so the word sits swallowed within the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the surname and the next two words

explanation.surface: A Russian aristocrat downing wine in the Siberian city of Omsk.
explanation.walkthrough: The Romanovs were Russia's royal dynasty and Omsk is a Siberian city, which sets a scene where vodka might be expected.
explanation.definitionFit: Vino is the Italian and Spanish word for wine, used informally in English for an everyday bottle.

clue.text: Test for the drinker, a table with sherry all over the place

indicators.note: something all over the place is in disarray, so the letters are scattered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A drinker's table is covered in spilled sherry, a sure sign of trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: The spilled sherry fits the drinking theme, which hides that the table and drink are the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A breathalyser is the roadside device police use to measure alcohol on a motorist's breath, so it tests anyone suspected of drinking.

clue.text: Substantial rope's held on bank, right?

indicators.note: something held is gripped from both sides, so one piece is enclosed by the other

parts.note: a cable is a thick rope
taken as written
a bank is the side of a river
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a hefty rope has been secured on the riverbank.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the apostrophe-s as 'has', not a possessive: the rope has held the other pieces, with a riverbank serving as a side.
explanation.definitionFit: Considerable means large in size or amount, the same sense as substantial, as in a considerable sum.

clue.text: Old mathematician God claims rang a bell

indicators.note: to claim something is to take hold of it, so one piece keeps another within it

parts.note: Ares is the Greek god of war
a bell that rang chimed

explanation.surface: An ancient scholar says that God claims the idea rang a bell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Claims' reads as a verb of speaking but acts as holding; 'rang a bell' suggests recognition, not a literal chime.
explanation.definitionFit: Archimedes of Syracuse was an ancient Greek scientist celebrated for his geometry and his principle of buoyancy.

clue.text: Old timer?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: previously owned, not new

definitions.note: a part of a timer rather than a whole timer
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the thin pointer on a clock face counting seconds

explanation.walkthrough: 'Old timer' looks like a veteran person; split, the words are two meanings of one hyphenated phrase, the question mark flagging the stretch from timer to its part.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods already used by a previous owner are described this way, and the same phrase names the fast pointer on a clock or watch.

clue.text: Plant computers correct again

parts.note: a reed is a tall grass-like waterside plant
IT is information technology, the field of computers

explanation.surface: An instruction to install computers and then fix them once more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks like a verb meaning install, but it is a noun naming a waterside grass.
explanation.definitionFit: To edit is to revise and fix errors in a text, so doing it a second time is to correct again.

clue.text: Repeater's funny funny conversation

indicators.note: funny can mean odd or peculiar, so the letters come out in a strange order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who repeats themselves keeps saying 'funny, funny' in conversation.
explanation.walkthrough: The doubled word looks like a typo or stammer; the first means strange, the second belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Repartee is quick, witty exchange of remarks, so it is talk that is clever and amusing.

clue.text: Where runner observed, tall thin person

definitions.note: a place, defined as a location rather than a thing
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the cane a runner bean climbs, where it can be seen growing
second meaning: a lanky, skinny individual

explanation.surface: A spectator spots a lanky athlete on the track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runner' suggests an athlete, but a runner is also a climbing bean, which grows up a garden cane.
explanation.definitionFit: Runner beans are trained up tall garden poles, and by comparison a very tall skinny person is given the same nickname.

clue.text: House done, Edward cleaned up

parts.note: HO is the abbreviation for house
something done is finished, over
Ed is a short form of Edward

explanation.surface: Edward has finished the housework and tidied up.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain Hoover, a vacuum cleaner brand, is the everyday verb for vacuuming, which fits Edward's housework.
explanation.definitionFit: To hoover a room is to vacuum it, so having hoovered means having removed the dust and dirt.

clue.text: Dark bruise, light?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: slang for a black eye
second meaning: something that gives off light

explanation.walkthrough: Dark and light look like opposites describing one bruise; the question mark marks the playful second sense of a thing that gleams.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally a black eye is called a shiner, and the word also literally means anything that glows or gleams.

clue.text: Mind item

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to be bothered by, to raise opposition
second meaning: a thing or article

explanation.walkthrough: 'Mind' looks like a noun for the intellect, but it is the verb used in 'do you mind?'.
explanation.definitionFit: If you mind something you protest against it, and separately the word is a noun for any physical thing or article.

clue.text: A prescription for fitness fanatics?

parts.note: surface reading: a doctor's order written for gym enthusiasts
setter's reading: a prescribed remedy combined with sporting equipment, naming a heavy weighted exercise sphere

explanation.walkthrough: A prescription is a doctor's medicine; the item meant is the heavy weighted ball thrown and caught in gym training.
explanation.definitionFit: This is weighted exercise equipment used for strength training, and its first word is what a doctor prescribes.

clue.text: Sage generally unwanted, rosemary usually for starters

indicators.note: starters come at the beginning of a meal, so only the opening letter of each word is used

parts.note: opening letter
opening letter
opening letter
opening letter

explanation.surface: A cook notes that sage is generally unwanted while rosemary is usually used in starters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sage' and 'rosemary' set a herb garden scene, but sage here means a wise person.
explanation.definitionFit: A guru is a respected spiritual teacher or expert, so it matches sage in its sense of a wise person.

clue.text: Church overcome by film score

indicators.note: in a down entry, something overcome by another lies beneath it, so it comes second

parts.note: E.T. is Spielberg's film about an extra-terrestrial
CH is the standard abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: A church choir is overwhelmed by the music of a film soundtrack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Score' seems to be a film's music, but it is a verb meaning to scratch a line into a surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To etch is to cut lines into metal or glass, and to score is likewise to mark a surface with a scratch.

clue.text: Honey at a high price

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a term of affection for a loved one

explanation.surface: A complaint that honey is sold expensively.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as costly honey from the shop; honey is in fact the pet name.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are affectionate forms of address, and in British usage something expensive is described as dear.

clue.text: A few drunken ultras flip!

parts.note: a few is some

indicators.note: someone drunken staggers about unsteadily, so the letters lurch into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A handful of drunken hardline football fans lose their temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flip!' looks like losing one's temper, but it is the acrobatic noun; ultras are fanatical football supporters.
explanation.definitionFit: A somersault is an acrobatic roll or leap turning heels over head, exactly the gymnastic move called a flip.

clue.text: Carbonated drink sent back in Colorado Springs

indicators.note: something sent back is returned the way it came, so it reads backwards
the letters sit inside the words that follow, unchanged

parts.note: the letters straddle the end of the state name and the start of the next word

explanation.surface: A fizzy drink is returned as unsatisfactory in a Colorado city.
explanation.walkthrough: Colorado Springs is a real US city, and 'Springs' even suggests water, which hides that the clue's letters are the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Soda is fizzy water or a sweet fizzy soft drink, so it is a straightforward synonym for a carbonated beverage.

clue.text: Clear sheet awfully coarse

indicators.note: awfully means in a terrible manner, so the letters are badly mangled

parts.note: taken as written
coarse means rough in texture

explanation.surface: Someone notes a bedsheet feels terribly rough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awfully coarse' reads as one phrase meaning very rough, but 'awfully' acts only on the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: See-through describes something transparent, which is what clear means when applied to glass or fabric.
